doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Preferred keys and key confusion on the bandstand
summary: Pallo prefers flat keys; they talk about Stardust and players who cannot name their key.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And they will go to B. And guitar players love E, we say — not all guitar players — love E, A and D let’s say. I hate those keys. Not that I hate them, I’d rather play E flat, it’s more for a horn. I like E flat, I like A flat, I love D flat. But E, because I got away from
that open stuff down there many, many years ago and it’s hard to me to even play the open chords anymore.
Well I think it’s hard. It’s hard.
I’d rather play all the different changes up here.
It’s hard. But that’s why I prefer E flat.
Well that puts you in good with most of the classic standards, because the majority of them are in flat keys, right?

Exactly. A flat, B flat, even “Stardust” is written in D flat, as you know. And then when you’re on a special gig you have to look over at the person that’s going to play it and say are you going to do it in the original or C? A lot of them do it in C.
They do it in C. But the original of course is D flat.
The worst is when they can’t tell you.

I’ve been through that too. I’ve been through that too, where I’ve asked many players, “What key are we in” and they just looked at me and I’m going wow you’re a horn player, but yet sometimes horns are a little different.
Right. Or sometimes they’ll say, “My first note is a D.”
Yes. I’ve been through that too.
So you’re thinking okay his first note’s a D [scats] do it like that, transposing.
